Oral mucositis

Recent randomized trials reported fewer severe cases with PBM during head-and-neck radiation and after transplantation. A 15-trial review and a separate seven-trial meta-analysis also favored PBM for severe mucositis, although protocols and populations varied.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Recent randomized trials reported fewer severe cases with PBM during head-and-neck radiation and after transplantation. A 15-trial review and a separate seven-trial meta-analysis also favored PBM for severe mucositis, although protocols and populations varied.

Summary of the Evidence

We identified 262 unique titles in the oral-mucositis category. The inventory includes clinical trials and observational reports, animal and laboratory studies, reviews, meta-analyses, protocols, editorials, guidelines, surveys, and other publication types. Method tags overlap, so type counts are not additive and publication count is not the number of independent cohorts. The literature includes repeated reports and varied cancer-treatment settings.

Human and clinical evidence

Two recent randomized trials illustrate direct clinical findings. In a multicenter sham-controlled trial across 12 US sites, intraoral LED PBM during intensity-modulated radiation therapy reduced severe oral mucositis during treatment and two weeks later. In the post-transplant POMFITT trial, severe mucositis was reported in 0% of the PBM group and 26.6% of controls, while physical function at discharge did not differ. Reviews synthesize, rather than add, primary cohorts: a 2026 review of 15 randomized trials and 868 adults found favorable pooled outcomes for severe mucositis and pain; a separate seven-trial meta-analysis of 329 participants also reported fewer severe cases (Hu et al. 2026 López-Espinoza et al. 2026 Parra-Rojas et al. 2026 Rojas et al. 2026).

Animal evidence

The database contains 24 animal-study records, with tags for hamster, rat, mouse, and cat models. Species tags may overlap and do not represent 25 separate experiments. These models examine tissue injury and mucosal healing but do not establish clinical efficacy.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

Three records are tagged as in-vitro studies. They are distinct laboratory evidence from the patient trials; biomarker measurements within an animal or clinical report are not counted as separate cell experiments.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Protocols vary by cancer treatment, oral sites, wavelength, light source, fluence, exposure time, and session timing. Hu and colleagues used intraoral LED treatment for 600 seconds daily immediately before intensity-modulated radiation therapy across six to eight weeks. The differing transplant, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy settings, as well as local treatment schedules, limit direct pooling of individual protocols.

Interpretation

Randomized trials and pooled analyses support reduced severe mucositis in selected cancer-treatment settings. The large evidence base is clinically relevant, but variation in protocols and populations limits a single effect estimate for every setting.

Evidence strength in source summarySevere oral mucositis during cancer therapy: Moderate for selected protocols Pain and duration across settings: Low to moderate
Publications and records262 unique titles; database classification tags overlap

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The category contains many trials and reviews, with overlapping method tags and protocols that vary by cancer treatment, light source, and schedule. Recent sham-controlled trials report fewer severe cases in specific treatment settings, while pooled estimates also favor PBM. The size and durability of benefit across regimens remain less certain than the results within those trials.
